In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radiative transport theory provides a very good approximation for the scattering by composite particle surfaces in the high porosities limit.
the classical radiative theory coupled with the assumption of a random particle distribution provides a good approximation of the light scattering by a planetary surface in the high porosities limit.
the classical radiative theory is adequate for the calculation of light scattering by surfaces of high porosity (greater than 50%) but not for surfaces of lower porosity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of the composite particle on the light scattering are significant and cannot be ignored.

radiative transfer theory can still be used to model light scattering by composite particles, but only in the limit where the scattering particles are well separated and the scattering by the composite particle is dominated by the scattering from the internal inclusions.
the classical radiative theory is not a good approximation for the scattering by composite particle containing multiple internal scatterers in a planetary surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, as in the earlier study, radiative transfer theory can provide a reasonable approximation of the scattering by a surface containing composite particles, but only in the limit of very high porosities.
the classical radiative theory should be applied with care to surfaces containing composite particles and that the results should always be checked against a more detailed model.
